Consult Summary:
- Acute asthma exacerbation with recent dyspnea on exertion, wheeze, and cough; plan includes interim inhaled therapy adjustment and urgent GP review; guidance on red-flag symptoms and escalation to urgent care if needed.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Shortness of breath with wheeze and cough for ~2–3 days; inability to relieve symptoms with blue inhaler.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began 2–3 days ago; previously asthma generally controlled; last significant attack ~3–4 years ago.
- Associated/concerning symptoms: No sputum production. No fever reported (hay fever/allergic rhinitis noted).
- Past medical history: Asthma; eczema; hay fever.
- Medications (as stated): 
  - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) used as needed and additionally morning/evening for prevention; used up to every 2–4 hours during symptoms.
  - Brown inhaler (Clenil) used as preventer; current use described as three puffs twice daily; plan to increase to four puffs twice daily.
  - Topicals: Hydrocortisone; Cetraben (emollient); Flanel Bactroban mentioned by patient (inconsistency noted later).
- Allergies: No drug allergies reported; patient mentions hay fever; “fever” misheard earlier.
- Social history/preventive care: Last asthma review with nurse ~2 years ago.

Examination:
- Not documented in transcript. No vitals provided. Chest exam and peak flow planned but not yet performed.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation on a background of otherwise controlled asthma; possible need for antibiotics/steroids depending on examination findings.

Plan:
- Interim management:
  - Increase Clenil (brown inhaler) to four puffs twice daily.
  - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed up to every 2 hours (max advised 2–4 hours); if symptoms worsen or persist, proceed to emergency care.
  - If breathing worsens or not improving, go to A&E.
- Diagnostics/Follow-up:
  - In-clinic chest examination with peak flow measurement.
  - Depending on findings, may require antibiotics and/or steroids.
  - Arrange GP appointment within the next few days for formal asthma assessment (face-to-face recommended).
  - Continue interim management while awaiting appointment.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Documentation of vital signs (BP, HR, RR, O2 saturation), if available.
  - Complete allergy/medication reconciliation (conflicting medication names noted in transcript; Flanel Bactroban vs Cetraben conflict).
  - Smoking status and immunization history.
- Internal conflicts noted:
  - Conflicting medication names: patient mentions Flanel Bactroban; later repeats Cetraben (emollient) with Hydrocortisone; also unclear exact inhaled medications beyond Clenil and Salbutamol.
  - Hay fever vs fever miscommunication in the interview.
- Transcript quality:
  - Some passages are noisy/unclear; several medication names and doses are inconsistently stated. Information requires clarification during formal review.
